name: English Opening
tagline: 1.c4 – you take d5 with a wing pawn, fianchetto the bishop on g2 and play a slow, squeezing game. Often it is a Sicilian with an extra move for you.
ideas: **The g2 bishop is the soul of the English.** After g3 and Bg2 it looks down the long diagonal at d5 and b7. Most of your plans make this bishop stronger.
Against **1...e5** you are playing a **Sicilian with colours reversed – and one extra move**. Black gets the centre; you attack it from the side.
Queenside play is normal: **Rb1, a3 and b4-b5** push Black's knight away from c6 and open lines for your rook and bishop.
Keep the d-pawn flexible. **d3** is solid, **d4** comes later when it opens lines for your pieces.
Watch the **...Nd4 jump**. Black's knight on d4 is strong, so often you trade it (Nxd4) or kick it with e3.

lines.name: Four Knights: 4.g3 d5 (Reversed Dragon)
lines.intro: Black plays like a White player in the Sicilian: ...e5 and ...d5. You calmly fianchetto, then start your queenside pawn storm with a3 and b4.

moves.text: The **English Opening**. The c-pawn controls d5 without blocking your bishops.
Black takes the centre with the king's pawn – this is the most popular answer.
Develop and add a second control of d5.
Black develops and also eyes d5 and e4.
Develop and attack e5 at once.
Black defends e5. This is the **Four Knights English**.
Prepare **Bg2**. This bishop will press along the long diagonal on d5, c6 and b7.
Black opens the centre, like a Sicilian Dragon with colours reversed.
Trade your wing pawn for Black's centre pawn – a good deal, just like in the Sicilian.
Black recaptures. The knight on d5 is now looking at your Nc3.
The bishop arrives on the long diagonal and puts pressure on d5 and c6.
Black steps back so the knight is not in the bishop's line.
Castle before you open anything. Your king is safe behind the g2 bishop.
Black develops and prepares to castle.
A solid move: it controls e4 and opens the c1 bishop.
Prepare **b4**. You want to gain space on the queenside, where you are stronger.
Black develops and covers c4 and d5.
The pawn storm starts. Next comes **b5** to kick the c6 knight, then Bb2 and Rc1.

lines.summary: This is your typical English plan: Bg2 on the long diagonal, then a3-b4-b5 on the queenside, with Bb2, Rc1 and Qc2. Black has the centre, but you have the pressure. If Black plays ...a5, answer b5 and the knight on c6 must move.

lines.name: Four Knights: 4.g3 Bb4 and ...e4
lines.intro: Black pins your c3 knight and pushes ...e4 to chase your f3 knight. You get the bishop pair and break the pawn with f3.

moves.text: Black pins the c3 knight and threatens to take it, so your pawns get doubled.
Keep developing. Doubled pawns on c3 are fine here: you get the two bishops.
Black chases your knight away from the centre.
The best square. The knight attacks e4 and is not easy to chase.
Black takes the knight so that e4 is not attacked twice.
Recapture towards the centre. Your b-file opens for a rook.
Strike at the e4 pawn. You want to open the f-file and free your pieces.
Recapture with the knight; it comes back to the centre.
Black takes space in the centre.
Stop Black's pawn from going further and open the c1 bishop's diagonal.

lines.summary: You have the bishop pair and a strong centre with c3-d4. Plans: Bf4 or Bg5, Qd3 and e2-e4 later. Your c-pawns are a little weak, so do not let Black win c4 for free.

lines.name: Symmetrical: 1...c5 (the Botvinnik-style squeeze)
lines.intro: Black copies you. You win the race on the queenside with Rb1 and b4, because you move first.

moves.text: Your bishop takes the long diagonal.
Castle first – king safety before action.
The knight goes to e7 so the g7 bishop's diagonal stays open.
Solid. It also opens the c1 bishop.
Connect the rooks and prepare Rb1.
Prepare b4. In symmetrical positions, the side that opens a line first is usually better.
The rook goes behind the b-pawn before it moves.
Black develops the last minor piece.
The break. If Black takes, your rook on b1 gets an open file.

lines.summary: The idea is simple: Rb1, a3 and b4. With the g2 bishop and the b-file you press on Black's queenside. Keep the position closed in the centre until your pieces are ready.

lines.name: Against the King's Indian set-up: the Botvinnik (e4)
lines.intro: Black plays ...Nf6, ...g6, ...Bg7, ...O-O. You build a pawn chain c4-d3-e4 and put your knight on e2, so that f2-f4 is possible later.

moves.text: Develop and control d5 and e4.
Black prepares a King's Indian set-up.
Black's bishop takes the long diagonal.
The **Botvinnik set-up**: pawns on c4 and e4 take away d5 from Black's pieces.
The knight goes to e2, not f3, so the f-pawn stays free to push f4 later.
Castle. Your king is safe and the rook is ready to support f4.
Complete the chain c4-d3-e4. The c1 bishop can now develop.
Prepare Be3 without ...Ng4 hitting it. Later you play f4 and Be3.

lines.summary: A stable, simple structure. Your plan is Be3, Qd2 and f2-f4 on the kingside; Black plays ...b5 on the queenside. Do not rush: the e4/c4 pawns keep Black's pieces off d5.

lines.name: 4...Nd4: just develop with 5.Bg2
lines.intro: Black jumps to d4. It looks like e5 is free, but it is not (see the trap line). You simply keep developing.

moves.text: Black jumps forward. The e5 pawn now looks unprotected.
Do not grab on e5. Finish your development; the d4 knight will be exchanged anyway.
Recapture. Your bishop is fine on f3 and can return to g2 later.
Castle first. Your king is safe and you avoid any tricks on the e-file.
Solid. Next you can play Bg2, a3 and b4 to gain queenside space.

lines.summary: A calm equal position where your bishop pair and queenside space give you easy play. The lesson: when an early pawn looks free in the English, check the e-file and the ...Nf3 square first.

lines.name: Trap warning: 5.Nxe5? Qe7! 6.Nd3?? Nf3#
lines.intro: A famous English trap that White falls into. Learn it so you never play it: after 4...Nd4, taking on e5 is risky, and 6.Nd3?? allows mate in one.

moves.text: Black jumps forward and sets a trap.
**Dubious (?)**: you grab the pawn, but your knight is now alone in the centre and your king is still on e1. Best was 5.Bg2.
The queen attacks the e5 knight **and** pins the e2 pawn to your king.
**Blunder (??)**: the knight retreats, but now the e2 pawn is pinned and cannot take on f3. Correct was 6.f4.
**Checkmate.** The knight checks from f3, the e2 pawn cannot capture because it is pinned by the queen, and your king has no squares.

lines.summary: Remember the pattern: queen on the e-file + knight jumping to f3 or d3 = mate when the e-pawn is pinned. In the English, 4...Nd4 is answered by 5.Bg2, not 5.Nxe5.

name: King's Indian Attack
tagline: Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, d3, Nbd2, e4 – one set-up against the French, the Caro-Kann and the Sicilian ...e6. Then e5 and a kingside attack.
ideas: **Same set-up every game**: Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, d3, Nbd2, e4 and Re1. You learn plans, not long move lists.
**The e5 push** is the key moment: it gains space, kicks Black's f6 knight, and makes room for your attack on the king.
The knight goes on a long trip: **Nd2-f1-h2-g4** (or Nf1-e3). With h4, Bf4 and Qe2 it builds pressure near Black's king.
Black usually attacks on the queenside with **...b5-b4 and ...a5-a4**. You must be faster on the kingside.
**Move order matters**: if Black has a bishop on c8, do not let ...Bg4 come with a pin before Nf3 – and check if a bishop on g4 is simply hanging to your queen.

lines.name: Against the French: e5, Nf1 and h4
lines.intro: The classic KIA. Black builds a French centre; you push e5 and attack on the kingside while Black runs on the queenside.

moves.text: Start with 1.e4. Against 1...e6 you can play the KIA instead of the main lines.
The KIA move: a solid pawn on d3 supports e4 and keeps the centre closed.
Defend e4 with the knight. Later it goes to f1 and h2.
Black takes space on the queenside.
The bishop supports e4 and protects your king.
Castle. Your king is safe before the position opens.
The rook supports e4 and later the e5 push.
**The key push.** You kick the f6 knight away from your king and gain space.
Black's knight has to step back.
The knight starts its trip to h2 and g4.
Gain space and prepare Bf4 and N1h2-g4. The h-pawn also stops ...g5.
The knight goes to h2 so it can jump to g4 and support the attack.

lines.summary: Typical plans: Ng4, Bf4, Qe2 or h5-h6 to weaken Black's king. Black will play ...a4-a3. Count the race: you must create threats before Black opens your queenside.

lines.name: Against the Sicilian 2...e6
lines.intro: The same plan works against the Sicilian when Black plays ...e6 and ...d5. It becomes a French with an extra ...c5 for Black.

moves.text: KIA set-up: d3 and later g3.
Kick the f6 knight and gain space.
Start the knight trip to h2 or e3.
Space on the kingside; next N1h2, Bf4 and Ng4.

lines.summary: This is almost the French line. Remember: e5 + Nf1-h2-g4 + h4 + Bf4. If Black plays ...f6 to break your e5 pawn, take on f6 and use the open e-file.

lines.name: Against the Caro-Kann: 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 e5
lines.intro: Black takes the centre with ...e5. You keep your structure and play for c3 and d4 later, or for Nc4 and a4.

moves.text: The KIA way against the Caro-Kann. You avoid all the main-line theory.
The bishop guards e4 and your king.
Prepare d4 or Qc2 and b4. This also takes d4 and b4 from Black's pieces.

lines.summary: A slow position, about equal. Plans: Qc2, Nh4-f5, or exd5 and d4 when Black's centre gets loose. Black has more space, so open the centre only when your pieces are ready.

lines.name: 1.Nf3 move order vs ...d5, ...c5 and ...e5
lines.intro: If you start with 1.Nf3, Black can build the best anti-KIA set-up: a reversed King's Indian with ...c5 and ...e5. Know it, and play Nc4 and a4.

moves.text: The flexible start. You can choose the KIA later.
KIA style. Note: d4 is a bit more active here, but d3 keeps the plan simple.
Black has a big centre – this is a King's Indian with colours reversed.
Challenge the centre. Now Black must decide about d5.
Pressure on e5 and support of e4.
Black closes the centre and gains space.
Fix Black's queenside pawns and give your knight the c4 square.

lines.summary: This is Black's most ambitious answer and the engine says Black is fine. Your plan: Nc4, a4-a5, and later f4 or Nh4-f5. It is a long manoeuvring game – good practice for understanding pawn chains.

lines.name: 1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bg4: h3 and e4
lines.intro: Black develops the bishop to g4 to pin your knight. You ask the question with h3 and then hit the centre with e4.

moves.text: Black develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and pins the knight.
Your bishop protects the king and the long diagonal.
Ask the bishop: take on f3 (giving you the bishop pair) or go back.
Strike at the centre. Later g4 and Nh4 can trap or trade the h5 bishop.

lines.summary: Equal and playable. Ideas: Qe1, Nh4, and g4 to chase the h5 bishop, or exd5 to open the e-file. Black's bishop on h5 can become a target.

lines.name: Trap: 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 Bg4?? 4.Qxg4
lines.intro: Caro-Kann players love ...Bg4. But in the KIA move order your knight is still on g1, so the d1-g4 diagonal is open.

moves.text: Defend e4. Notice: your queen on d1 now sees e2, f3, g4 and h5.
**Blunder (??)**. Black plays the usual Caro-Kann move, but there is no knight on f3 to pin.
Take the free bishop. Always check if a 'pinning' move actually pins something.
Step back. You are a full piece up.

lines.summary: Easy point: when an opponent plays a move 'from memory', check whether it still works in this move order. Here the bishop on g4 was just hanging.

name: Jobava London
tagline: 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4 – the aggressive cousin of the London. The knight on c3 threatens Nb5 and Nxc7, and you often castle long and attack.
ideas: **The c7 square is Black's weak point.** Your Bf4 already hits it; **Nb5** hits it a second time. Many Black players lose material right here.
Against ...e6 and ...c5 you often play **Nb5** to provoke ...Na6, then c3 and Bd3 like a London.
Against ...Bf5 you can be aggressive: **f3, g4 and h4** chase the bishop, and you castle long.
The pawn on **c2 is blocked** by the c3 knight, so you rarely play c4. Your play is in the centre and on the kingside.
Your **light-squared bishop** goes to d3 or b5. Trading it for Black's f5 or g6 bishop is fine.

lines.name: Main line vs 3...e6: 4.Nb5 Na6
lines.intro: Black plays solidly with ...e6. You use the Nb5 threat to put Black's knight on a6, then build a London-style centre.

moves.text: The Jobava move. The knight is active and eyes **b5**.
Now c7 is attacked by the bishop, and Nb5 would attack it a second time.
Black defends c7. The knight on a6 is not a great square.
Open your f1 bishop and support d4.
The bishop aims at h7 – your attacking diagonal.
Support d4 with a pawn. Your knight on b5 can come back to c3 or go to a3 later.

lines.summary: A healthy London-type position. Plans: Qe2, Ne5, h4 or O-O and a kingside attack. Black's knight on a6 needs time to come back into play.

lines.name: 3...c5: 4.e3 cxd4 5.exd4
lines.intro: Black hits the centre at once. After exd4 you get an open e-file and an easy game.

moves.text: Support d4 and open the f1 bishop.
Recapture with the e-pawn. You get the open e-file and a strong bishop on f4.
Develop calmly. (Bd3 lets ...Bg4 pin your knight with more effect.)
Jump forward and break the pin. Trading on e2 or e5 is fine for you.

lines.summary: Equal, with clear plans: Re1, Ne5, and a later c3 or Nb1-d2. Black has an isolated-looking structure in the centre, so endgames are fine for you.

lines.name: 3...Bf5: the f3-g4-h4 attack
lines.intro: Black copies your bishop move. You chase the bishop with your kingside pawns and castle long. Sharp and fun, about equal.

moves.text: Prepare g4 to chase the bishop, and later e4.
Black makes room for the bishop on h7.
Open your f1 bishop and support d4.
Castle long. Your pawns go forward on the kingside while your king is on the other side.

lines.summary: Opposite-side castling means a pawn race. Your plan: h5, g5, Bd3 and Nge2. Black plays ...Nc6, ...Qa5 and ...b5. The engine says equal, so speed decides.

lines.name: 3...g6: 4.Nb5 Na6
lines.intro: Against a fianchetto Black still has the c7 problem. You use Nb5 to put the knight on a6, then develop normally.

moves.text: Black defends c7 with the knight.
Black's bishop is on the long diagonal.
Make a hole for your bishop on h2 and stop ...Ng4 or ...Bg4.
The knight comes back to the centre. It did its job: Black's knight is on a6.

lines.summary: Equal and easy to play: Be2 or Bd3, O-O, Ne5 and c3 later. Black's a6 knight usually needs ...Nc7 to come back.

lines.name: Trap: 3...Nbd7? 4.Nb5! and Nxc7+
lines.intro: The most common mistake against the Jobava. Black blocks the d8 queen's defence of c7, and Nb5 wins material.

moves.text: **Mistake (?)**: the knight can no longer go to a6 to defend c7.
Now c7 is attacked twice (Nb5 and Bf4) and defended only once (the queen).
**Blunder (??)**: Black does not see the threat. The best defence was 4...e5!, giving a pawn.
Fork! The knight checks the king and attacks the rook on a8.
Black gives the queen to stop the fork.
You win the queen for a knight.

lines.summary: Remember: in the Jobava, ...Nbd7 before ...e6 or ...c6 is a mistake. Always look at c7 – it is the first target of the opening.

name: Anti-Sicilian: the Alapin (2.c3)
tagline: 1.e4 c5 2.c3 – prepare d4 so that you can recapture with a pawn and keep a big centre. Less theory than the Open Sicilian and a clear plan.
ideas: **The point of c3**: after d4 and ...cxd4, you take back with the **c-pawn** and keep two centre pawns.
Against **2...d5** the black queen comes to d5 early. You develop with **Nf3, Be2, O-O, Be3 and Nc3**, hitting the queen with tempo.
Against **2...Nf6** you push **e5** and chase the knight. Your pawn on e5 gives you space on the kingside.
You often get an **isolated d-pawn (IQP)**. That is fine: it gives you space and active pieces. Attack before the endgame.
Typical tactic: **d4-d5!** when a black piece on c6 or b4 is loose.

lines.name: 2...d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 Bg4
lines.intro: The most solid reply. Black's queen comes out early, so you develop and use tempo against it.

moves.text: Black hits e4 at once – the main line.
Take. Black must recapture with the queen.
The queen is in the centre, but it can be attacked later.
Build your centre. The c3 pawn will support d4.
Black pins the knight and puts pressure on d4.
Break the pin and prepare to castle.
Castle. Now the knight on f3 is no longer pinned to the king.
Recapture with the pawn. You have an **isolated d-pawn** and free development.
Develop with tempo on the queen.
Hit b7 and get the queen out. Next: Rad1 or Rfd1.

lines.summary: A typical IQP position. Plans: Rfd1, Ne5, a3 and sometimes d4-d5 to open lines. Keep pieces on the board – the IQP is strong in the middlegame and weaker in the endgame.

lines.name: 2...Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nf3
lines.intro: Black attacks e4 with the knight. You push e5 and use the space. 5.Nf3 keeps the option of taking on d4 later.

moves.text: Gain space and chase the knight.
The knight goes to the centre.
Develop first. You can take on d4 with the pawn or the knight later.
The knight steps back and attacks your bishop.
Keep the bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal, where it aims at f7.
Black attacks your e5 pawn from the side.
Take en passant. This opens the position for your faster development.
Win back the pawn. Your pieces are active and Black's king is still in the centre.

lines.summary: Material is equal. Plans: Re1 with tempo on the e6 queen, Nb5 or Nxc6, Bf4. Black must be careful because the e-file is open and the king has not castled.

lines.name: 2...Nf6 with 5.cxd4 d6 6.Nf3
lines.intro: The other way to handle 2...Nf6: take on d4 with the pawn and keep the strong e5 pawn as long as possible.

moves.text: The knight goes to the centre.
Take back with the pawn: now you have pawns on d4 and e5.
Black adds pressure on d4 and e5.
The knight steps back with tempo on your bishop.
Pin the c6 knight. Now it cannot defend e5 well.
Recapture with the knight – it is strong on e5 and attacks c6.
Take the bishop. You get the bishop pair.
Develop. Next: O-O, Be3 and Qg4 or d5.

lines.summary: You have the two bishops and an isolated d-pawn; Black is solid. Typical plans: O-O, Be3, Rc1 and d4-d5 at the right moment.

lines.name: 2...e6 3.d4 d5 4.exd5 exd5: IQP for Black
lines.intro: Black answers like a French. You play Bb5 and dxc5 so that Black gets an isolated pawn on d5 instead of you.

moves.text: Black recaptures. The e-file is open.
Pin the c6 knight. It can no longer defend d4 and c5 comfortably.
Take! Now Black's d5 pawn will be isolated.
Black develops and prepares to castle.
Head for b3 to attack the c5 bishop and control d4.
Hit the bishop and control the **d4 square** in front of the isolated pawn.
Take the open e-file. Next: Be3, Bd3 and Nbd4.

lines.summary: This time **Black** has the isolated d-pawn. Your plan: put a knight on d4 (the blockade square), trade some pieces and attack the d5 pawn in the endgame.

lines.name: 2...d6 3.d4 Nf6 4.Bd3: the big centre
lines.intro: Black plays slowly. You simply keep both centre pawns and develop.

moves.text: Stop ...Bg4 and ...Ng4. Your centre stays strong.
Support e4. Next: Nbd2-f1 or d5.

lines.summary: White is better here: two strong centre pawns and an easy game. Plans: d5 to kick the c6 knight, Nbd2, Bc2 and Qe2.

lines.name: Trap: 9...Qa5 10.a3 Nf6? 11.d5!
lines.intro: In the 2...d5 line Black often puts a bishop on b4 and the queen on a5. If Black is careless, d4-d5! opens the position and wins material.

moves.text: Develop with tempo on the queen.
Castle. The c3 knight is no longer pinned to your king.
Ask the b4 bishop: take or retreat?
**The key break!** The d-pawn attacks the c6 knight and opens the e-file and the a1-h8 diagonal.
Take the bishop. Black's queen can now take your rook on a1, but you will get two pieces for it.
Attack the c6 knight. Black's queen on a1 is nearly trapped and you have two pieces for a rook.

lines.summary: Remember the **d4-d5 break** in IQP positions: when black pieces stand on c6 and b4, the push opens lines and loose pieces fall. White is winning here.

name: Nimzo-Indian Defence
tagline: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 – pin the knight that wants to support e4. Often you give the bishop for the knight and fight against doubled c-pawns.
ideas: **The pin on c3 stops e2-e4.** The c3 knight is White's best defender of e4, so ...Bb4 is a fight for the centre, not just a check.
**...Bxc3 is a trade, not a gift.** You give the bishop pair; in return White often gets **doubled c-pawns** that you can attack with ...c5, ...b6, ...Ba6 and ...Na5.
Your light squares: **...b6 and ...Bb7 or ...Ba6**, and the knight on e4. Control e4 and White's centre cannot move.
Against **4.Qc2** White avoids doubled pawns; you play ...O-O, ...Bxc3 and ...d5 or ...b6 with a solid game.
If White plays an early **e4?!** without preparation, take it: ...Nxe4 is safe, but watch for Qg4 hitting g7.

lines.name: Rubinstein: 4.e3 O-O 5.Bd3 d5
lines.intro: White's most solid system. You castle, hit the centre with ...d5 and ...c5, and take on c4 at the right moment.

moves.text: The **Nimzo-Indian**. You pin the knight, so e4 is not possible for now.
The **Rubinstein**: White builds a solid centre and develops.
Castle first. Your king is safe and you keep all options.
White develops and aims at h7.
Take the centre. Now e4 is impossible.
Attack d4. This is the standard Nimzo pawn structure.
Develop and add pressure on d4.
Give the bishop for the knight. White gets doubled c-pawns.
Take the c4 pawn so the d3 bishop has to move again.
The queen prepares ...e5. It also watches the c4 bishop and the e5 square.

lines.summary: Your plan is **...e5**: after ...e5 and ...exd4 White's c3 pawn may become weak. White has the bishop pair and wants Ba2, Re1 and e4. A classic, balanced middlegame.

lines.name: Classical: 4.Qc2 O-O 5.a3 Bxc3+ 6.Qxc3 b6
lines.intro: White avoids doubled pawns by recapturing with the queen. You get fast development and play on the light squares.

moves.text: The **Classical**. White wants to recapture on c3 with the queen.
White has the bishop pair and no doubled pawns, but has spent many queen moves.
Prepare ...Bb7 to control e4 and the long diagonal.
Develop. Your bishop fights for e4.
Strike in the centre before White plays e4.
Develop and break the pin later with ...c5 or ...Re8.
Recapture with the knight. It hits the c3 queen and the queens may come off.
...and you take White's queen. Material is equal.
White's bishop escapes with tempo on your rook.
Your knight returns to the centre. The endgame is equal.

lines.summary: An equal endgame. White has the two bishops; you have a good knight on d5 and a healthy structure. Play ...c5 and ...Rac8 and use the c-file.

lines.name: Sämisch: 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.bxc3 c5
lines.intro: White forces the trade on c3 at once and gets doubled pawns plus the bishop pair. You block the centre and attack the c4 pawn.

moves.text: The **Sämisch**. White says: take my knight now.
You take. White gets doubled c-pawns.
White recaptures and has the bishop pair.
Fix the doubled pawns: the c4 pawn will become a target.
The knight goes to e2 so the f-pawn can support e4.
Prepare **...Ba6** to attack the weak c4 pawn.
A clever retreat (Capablanca's idea): ...f5 is next, so White's e4-e5 does not hit your knight.

lines.summary: Plans: ...Ba6, ...Na5 and ...Rc8 to win the c4 pawn, and ...f5 to stop White's attack. White plays f4-f5 on the kingside. Sharp but logical.

lines.name: 4.Nf3 O-O 5.Bg5 c5
lines.intro: White develops normally. You hit d4 with ...c5 and get a typical isolated-pawn position for White.

moves.text: White recaptures. This structure gives White an isolated d-pawn after ...d5 and ...dxc4.
White adds a defender to c3.
Take: White's d4 pawn is now isolated.
Retreat the bishop and break the pin on f6.

lines.summary: White has an isolated d-pawn (IQP). Your plan: block it with a knight on d5, trade pieces, and attack the pawn in the endgame. Play ...b6, ...Bb7 and ...Rc8.

lines.name: 4.f3 d5 5.a3 Bxc3+ 6.bxc3 c5
lines.intro: White prepares e4 with f3. You hit the centre first with ...d5 and ...c5.

moves.text: Attack the centre from the side.
Recapture with the knight. It is strong on d5 and hits c3.
Attack c3 and c5. You will win the pawn back.

lines.summary: Black is fine. Next ...Qxc5 or ...Nd7xc5, then ...O-O. White's pawn on c3 and the e3 square are weak; White's bishops are the compensation.

name: Queen's Indian / Bogo-Indian (vs 3.Nf3)
tagline: When White avoids the Nimzo with 3.Nf3, you choose: 3...Bb4+ (Bogo-Indian, simple) or 3...b6 (Queen's Indian, control of e4 with the bishop).
ideas: These are the **partners of the Nimzo-Indian**: after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 there is no knight on c3 to pin, so you need another plan.
**Bogo-Indian (3...Bb4+)**: an easy check. Usually you trade the dark-squared bishops and play ...d6 and ...e5, or ...d5.
**Queen's Indian (3...b6)**: the bishop goes to **b7 or a6** and controls **e4 and the long diagonal**. Very solid.
Your favourite outpost is **e4** for the knight, and your favourite break is **...c5** (or ...e5 in the Bogo).
Do not fear trades: the pawn structure is healthy, so equal endgames are fine for you.

name: Grünfeld Defence

The **g7 bishop** is your best piece. Never trade it lightly – it pressures d4 and the long diagonal to a1.
In the **Exchange Variation** (4.cxd5 Nxd5 5.e4 Nxc3 6.bxc3) White gets c3-d4-e4. You play ...c5 and often trade queens: the endgame is fine for you.
Typical tactic: **...Qa5+ and ...Bxc3+** when the c3 pawn or the a1 rook is loose.
Honest note: the Grünfeld needs **a lot of theory**. Below 1800 the QGD or Slav gives you the same results with less memory work.

name: Dutch Defence: Leningrad and Stonewall
tagline: 1.d4 f5 – control e4 with a pawn from move one and play for a kingside attack. Leningrad (...g6, ...Bg7) is dynamic; Stonewall (...e6, ...d5, ...c6) is a fortress.
ideas: **1...f5 fights for e4.** It also weakens your king a little (the e8-h5 diagonal) – so watch Qh5+ tricks and Bg5 lines.
**Leningrad**: ...Nf6, ...g6, ...Bg7, ...O-O, ...d6 and **...e5**. It is a King's Indian with an extra f-pawn move. The queen often goes to **e8** and then h5 or f7.
**Stonewall**: pawns on **c6, d5, e6, f5**. Your knight sits on **e4**, your bishop on d6. The weak square is e5 and your c8 bishop is passive – plan ...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7-e8-h5.
Against early **Bg5** (anti-Dutch) you can chase it with ...h6 and ...g5 – but never with the king exposed to **Qh5#**.
Honest note: 1...f5 is a fighting choice. Stockfish says White is a little better, but at club level it gives many winning chances.

lines.intro: White gives a pawn to open lines. You keep it with ...Nc6 and ...Ne5-f7 and return it at the right time.

name: Pirc and Modern Defence
tagline: 1.e4 d6 (Pirc) or 1.e4 g6 (Modern) – give White the centre, fianchetto your bishop, and strike back later with ...e5 or ...c5. Flexible, but you must know White's attacks.
ideas: **Hypermodern idea**: you do not take the centre at once. You let White build e4-d4 and attack it later with **...e5, ...c5 or ...b5**.
The **g7 bishop** is the heart of your position. Against the 150 Attack (Be3, Qd2, Bh6) White tries to trade it – be ready.
Against the **Austrian Attack (f4)** strike fast with ...c5 or ...Na6-c5; do not let White push e5 for free.
**Modern (1...g6)**: you delay ...Nf6, so White's e5 push does not hit anything. Plans with ...a6, ...b5 and ...Bb7 (Tiger's Modern).
Danger: early **e5** tricks against a knight on f6. Never put a knight on a square where a bishop can take it (like ...Nd5?? with Bc4).

lines.name: Modern: 1...g6 2.d4 Bg7 3.Nc3 d6 4.Be3 a6

name: Sicilian Najdorf: 6.Bg5, 6.Bc4, 6.f4, 6.g3
tagline: Deeper Najdorf for 1700+. The basic Sicilian course covers 6.Be2 and 6.Be3; here are White's other main attacks, plus a famous trap.
ideas: Against **6.Bg5** play **...e6**: the f6 knight is pinned, so you must be ready for f4-e5. Black's main choices are ...Be7 (classical) or ...Qb6 (Poisoned Pawn).
Against **6.Bc4** (Fischer-Sozin) play **...e6 and ...b5**: blunt the bishop and gain queenside space with tempo.
Against **6.f4** and **6.g3** play **...e5**: White's knight must leave d4, and the d5 square is the key square for both sides.
Typical Najdorf ideas: **...b5-b4** to kick the c3 knight, **...Nbd7-c5** to hit e4, and **...Rc8** with pressure on c3 (sometimes ...Rxc3!).

lines.name: Trap: 6.Be3 e5 7.Nf5? d5! 8.exd5?? Bxf5
lines.intro: After 6.Be3 e5 the knight must go to b3, f3 or e2. Many players jump to f5 – it looks strong, but ...d5! wins a piece if White is careless.

moves.text: Trade your c-pawn for White's d-pawn – the Sicilian deal.
The **Najdorf**. It stops Nb5 and Bb5 and prepares ...e5 or ...b5.
The English Attack set-up (see the Sicilian course).
**Mistake (?)**: the knight looks active, but it is only defended by the e4 pawn.
Attack e4 – the only defender of f5. Also your c8 bishop now sees f5.
**Blunder (??)**: White takes, but now nothing defends f5. Better was 8.Bg5.
Take the knight. You are a piece up for a pawn.
White recaptures. Next ...Bb4 or ...Bd6 and ...O-O; you are winning.

lines.summary: Pattern: when a white knight on f5 is defended only by the e4 pawn, **...d5!** attacks the defender. Count defenders of every advanced piece.

name: Accelerated Dragon (and the Maróczy Bind)
tagline: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 – a Dragon without ...d6, so you can play ...d5 in one move. The test is the Maróczy Bind (5.c4).
ideas: **Why accelerated?** Without ...d6 you can play **...d7-d5 in one move**, which kills the Yugoslav Attack plans (Be3, f3, Qd2, O-O-O).
The **g7 bishop** and the **c-file** are your weapons. Trade on d4 with ...Nxd4 to open the bishop's diagonal.
**Maróczy Bind (5.c4)**: White gets pawns on c4 and e4 and a grip on d5. You do not need to break it at once – play ...d6, ...Be6, ...Qa5, ...Rfc8 and **...a6-b5** or **...f5** later.
The **...Ng4! trick** against Be3: ...Ng4 hits the e3 bishop, and after Qxg4 Nxd4 the knight is strong.
Danger: the **Na5? e5 and Bxf7+** trap (Fischer). Know it before you play this opening.

lines.name: Maróczy Bind: 5.c4 Nf6 6.Nc3 d6 7.Be2 Nxd4
lines.intro: The main line. White grips d5 with c4 and e4. You trade knights, put the queen on a5 and play on the queenside.

moves.text: The **Accelerated Dragon**: the bishop goes to g7 before you play ...d6, so ...d5 in one move stays possible.
The **Maróczy Bind**: White's c4 and e4 pawns control d5.
Trade knights. This gives your g7 bishop more room.
Develop – the bishop hits the queen on d4.
Develop and put pressure on c4.
The queen goes to a5: it hits c3 and a2 and supports ...Rfc8.
Put the rook on the c-file.
White protects c4 with a pawn.

lines.summary: Equal. Your plan: ...b5 (sometimes as a pawn sacrifice), or ...Nd7-c5 and ...Qb4. White is solid; be patient – the Maróczy is a long game.

lines.name: Maróczy Bind: 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 Ng4!
lines.intro: When White plays Be3 before Be2, the ...Ng4 trick is available. You trade White's best bishop or win time.

moves.text: The **Accelerated Dragon**: the bishop goes to g7 before you play ...d6, so ...d5 in one move stays possible.
Develop first – now the d4 knight is attacked.
**The trick.** You attack the e3 bishop.
...but now your knight takes d4 and threatens ...Nc2+, forking king and rook. Material is equal.
The queen goes back to cover c2.
The knight retreats to a safe, strong square.
White defends c3 and the c-file.
The queen pins c3 and eyes a2.

lines.summary: Easy equality: you traded a pair of knights, your g7 bishop is strong, and the e4 pawn is under pressure. A very useful line to know.

lines.name: Classical: 5.Nc3 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Bc4 Qa5
lines.intro: White plays like a Yugoslav Attack. Your queen goes to a5 to pin c3 and prepare ...Ng4 or ...d5 tricks.

moves.text: The **Accelerated Dragon**: the bishop goes to g7 before you play ...d6, so ...d5 in one move stays possible.
Pin the c3 knight to the king. Now e4 is only defended by a pinned knight, so ...Nxe4 is a threat.
White castles short and unpins the knight.
Now ...d6 is fine: White has castled short, so there is no Yugoslav attack.
White gains space on the kingside.

lines.summary: Equal. Plans: ...Nxd4 and ...Bc6 to hit e4, ...Rac8 and ...Qh5. The engine likes ...Nxd4 here.

lines.name: Classical: 7.Be2 O-O 8.O-O d5!
lines.intro: White plays quietly with Be2. You use the accelerated idea: ...d5 in one move frees your game.

moves.text: The **Accelerated Dragon**: the bishop goes to g7 before you play ...d6, so ...d5 in one move stays possible.
**The point of the Accelerated Dragon**: ...d5 in one move.
Recapture with the queen – it is safe because the g7 bishop hits d4.
The queen goes to c4, where it is safe and active.

lines.summary: Equal and comfortable. Black has no weaknesses and the g7 bishop pressures d4 and b2. Plans: ...Rd8, ...Bf5 and ...Nxd4.

lines.name: 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.Qd4 Nf6 7.e5 Nd5
lines.intro: White trades on c6 and attacks with the queen. You stay calm and give back the d7 pawn to develop quickly.

moves.text: The **Accelerated Dragon**: the bishop goes to g7 before you play ...d6, so ...d5 in one move stays possible.
White trades knights and doubles your pawns.
Recapture towards the centre. The b-file is open for your rook.
Block the long diagonal and develop.
White tries to break your structure.
Do not take: keep the f-file closed and the king safe.
Recapture. You are developed and have the bishop pair.

lines.summary: Equal. Plans: ...e5, ...Bg7 or ...Bd6, ...Rb8 and ...O-O. Your centre pawns are strong.

lines.name: Trap warning: 8...Na5? 9.e5 Ne8?? 10.Bxf7+! (Fischer)
lines.intro: A famous trap, played by Fischer. Black attacks the b3 bishop, but e5 and Bxf7+ win the queen.

moves.text: The **Accelerated Dragon**: the bishop goes to g7 before you play ...d6, so ...d5 in one move stays possible.
**Mistake (?)**: you want to trade the b3 bishop, but now e5 is strong. Correct was 8...d6 or 8...a5.
**Blunder (??)**: the knight leaves the defence of d7 and the queen's diagonal. Better was 9...Nxb3.
The bishop sacrifice! It removes the f7 pawn and pulls your king forward.
The knight jumps in and attacks your queen on d8.

lines.summary: Remember: in the Accelerated Dragon, **do not play ...Na5 before ...d6**. If you do, e5 + Bxf7+ + Ne6 wins your queen.

name: Against the English and Réti (as Black)
tagline: 1.c4 and 1.Nf3 – meet the English with 1...e5 (a Sicilian with colours reversed) and the Réti with 1...d5 and a Slav set-up (...c6, ...Bf5, ...e6).
ideas: Against **1.c4** play **1...e5**: you take the centre and get a 'reversed Sicilian'. Plan ...Nf6, ...Nc6, ...Bb4 or ...d5.
Against **1.Nf3** play **1...d5**: if White plays d4 later you are in your QGD/Slav repertoire. If White plays c4, answer **...c6** (Slav set-up).
Against fianchetto set-ups, the **Slav triangle c6-d5-e6** with **...Bf5 or ...Bg4 outside the chain** is the simplest structure.
Move orders: 1.c4 e6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d4 is just a QGD. Use your 1.d4 repertoire whenever White transposes.
Typical tactic in the English: **...Nd4 with ...Qe7** against a knight on e5 – Nd3?? allows **...Nf3#**.

lines.name: 1.c4 e5 Four Knights: 4.g3 Bb4 and 9...e3!?
lines.intro: You pin the c3 knight and push ...e4. If White plays f3, the pawn sacrifice ...e3 leaves White with weak pawns.

moves.text: Take the centre: a Sicilian with colours reversed.
Pin the knight that controls d5 and e4.
Chase the f3 knight from the centre.
Remove the knight that also attacks e4.
**A pawn sacrifice**: the pawn on e3 cramps White and blocks the c1 bishop.
Open your c8 bishop. White has an extra pawn but doubled, weak pawns on c3, c4 and e3.

lines.summary: Equal. Your plan: ...Ne5 to attack c4, ...Bf5 or ...Be6, ...Qe7. White's extra pawn is hard to use because the pawns are weak.

lines.name: 1.c4 e5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 d5: Reversed Dragon
lines.intro: You play a Sicilian Dragon as White would. Your knight goes to b6 and your bishop to e6; watch White's b4-b5 plan.

moves.text: Take the centre with both pawns.
Retreat out of the g2 bishop's line.
Hit the b4 pawn at once.
The knight jumps to the strong d4 square.

lines.summary: Equal. Your knight on d4 is strong; trade it only for White's f3 knight. Plans: ...f6, ...Qd7 and ...Rad8. White plays Bb2 and Nd2.

lines.name: 1.c4 e5 Four Knights: 4.e3 Bb4 5.Qc2
lines.intro: White plays the quiet e3 set-up. You trade on c3 and play ...d5 to free your game.

moves.text: White unpins and prepares Nd5 or a3.
Trade the knight that controls d5.

lines.summary: Equal. White has the bishop pair; you have the centre. Plans: ...O-O, ...Rd8 and ...Bg4 or ...f5.

lines.name: 1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 c6: Slav set-up vs the Réti
lines.intro: Against the Réti you build the Slav triangle and develop your bishop to f5 before ...e6.

moves.text: White attacks d5 from the side.
Support d5 with the c-pawn – a Slav set-up.
Develop the bishop outside the pawn chain **before ...e6**.
White prepares Bb2: a double fianchetto.
Give your bishop a safe square on h7 if White plays Nh4.

lines.summary: Equal and very solid. Plans: ...a5-a4, ...Bh7 and ...Qe7. If White plays e4, answer ...dxe4 or ...Bh7 and keep your structure.

lines.name: 1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bg4: against the KIA
lines.intro: Against the King's Indian Attack you develop the bishop to g4 and build a big centre with ...c6 and ...e5.

moves.text: Develop the bishop and pin the knight.
Take the centre with both pawns.

lines.summary: Equal. You have a nice centre and active bishops. Watch out for g4 and Nh4 trying to trap or trade your h5 bishop – keep g6 available.

lines.name: Trap: 4...Nd4 5.Nxe5? Qe7! 6.Nd3?? Nf3#
lines.intro: A trap you can set in the English Four Knights. If White takes on e5, the queen pins the e2 pawn and a knight check is mate.

moves.text: Jump forward. The e5 pawn looks free – this is the bait.
Attack the e5 knight **and** pin the e2 pawn to the king.
**Blunder (??)**: White saves the knight but forgets the pin. 6.f4 was necessary.
**Checkmate.** The e2 pawn cannot take because it is pinned by your queen.

lines.summary: If White finds 6.f4, there is no mate, but you are slightly better: play ...d6 and win back the pawn. Pattern: queen on the e-file + pinned e2 pawn + knight jumping to f3 = mate.

name: Caro-Kann: Advance and Exchange, deeper
tagline: The next step after the basic Caro-Kann course: White's sharp Advance tries (4.Nc3 with g4, 4.h4, 6.Be3) and the slow Exchange with Bd3 and c3.
ideas: In the **Advance** your two key moves are **...e6 and ...c5**: always attack the base of White's pawn chain (d4).
Against **g4 and h4** pushes, keep a retreat for the f5 bishop (g6, h7) and hit back with **...h5** at the right moment.
The **Qb6 + ...Nc6 + ...cxd4** pressure on d4 and b2 is your main weapon when White plays Be3 or Be2.
In the **Exchange (Bd3, c3)** White's bishop stops ...Bf5. Play **...Nc6, ...Nf6, ...Bg4** or **...Qc7** to stop Bf4, then the **minority attack ...b5-b4**.
Do not open lines next to your own king: **never ...hxg4 when Nxg6 fxg6 wrecks your pawns** (see the warning line).

lines.name: Advance: 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4 Bg6 6.Nge2 c5 7.h4 h5
lines.intro: White's sharpest system. White chases your bishop with g4 and h4; you hit the centre with ...c5 and stop the h-pawn with ...h5.

moves.text: Develop the bishop outside the chain.
Open the f8 bishop and give the f5 bishop room to go back.
The bishop goes back but stays on the good diagonal.
Attack d4 – the base of White's chain.
White threatens h5 to trap the bishop.
Stop h5. Now White's pawns on g4 and h4 can become weak.
The knight attacks your g6 bishop.
Go back to h7; the bishop is safe and still active.
Take back in the centre: the d4 pawn was White's support.
Develop with tempo on the queen. You have good play for the pawn.

lines.summary: The engine likes Black here: White's king has no safe home and White's pieces are scattered. Plans: ...Qb6 or ...Bc5, ...Nge7-f5, and ...O-O-O. Note: if White plays 7.Be3 instead of 7.h4, play ...Nc6 and keep the bishop on h7 – see the warning line.

lines.name: Advance: 4.h4 h5 5.c4 e6
lines.intro: White pushes h4 to chase your bishop with h5 or g4. You stop it with ...h5, then fight the centre with ...e6, ...Ne7 and ...Nd7.

moves.text: Develop the bishop outside the chain.
White threatens g4 and h5 to trap the bishop.
Stop h5 and make g4 more difficult. The g4 square is now weak for White.
White attacks d5 from the side.
The knight goes to e7, where it supports d5 and can go to f5 or g6.
White prepares Ng3 to hit your bishop.
Keep the bishop on the long diagonal.

lines.summary: Equal. Plans: ...dxc4 and ...Nd5 or ...Nb6, and ...c5 to attack d4. The g4 square is your outpost – a knight or bishop can land there.

lines.name: Exchange: 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Qc7 (stop Bf4)
lines.intro: A clever move order: ...Qc7 stops White's Bf4. Then you can play ...e5 and get an active game.

moves.text: Stop **Bf4**: White's bishop has no good square now.
White develops the knight to e2 (so f3 is possible).
Develop with tempo on the e2 knight.
The bishop goes back. White's f3 pawn weakens e3 and the king.
White develops with tempo on your queen.
Strike in the centre – a pawn break with tempo.
Recapture. Your pieces are very active.

lines.summary: The engine likes Black. Plans: ...Bd6, ...Nf6, ...O-O and ...Rae8. White's f3 move made e3 weak.

lines.name: Exchange: 6.Bf4 Bg4 7.Nf3 e6 – the minority attack
lines.intro: White plays the quiet 7.Nf3 instead of 7.Qb3. You trade the dark bishops and start the minority attack with ...Rab8 and ...b5.

moves.text: White develops the bishop outside the chain.
Now play ...e6: the bishop is already out.
Offer to trade White's good bishop.
White's rook goes to the e-file.
Prepare **...b5-b4**: the **minority attack**. Two pawns attack three to create a weak pawn on c3.

lines.summary: Equal. Your plan: ...b5, ...b4 and ...bxc3 to leave White with a weak pawn on c3 or d4. White plays on the kingside with Ne5, Qe2 and Re3.

lines.name: Trap: 6.Be3 Qb6 7.Nbd2 Nc6 8.O-O? cxd4! 9.Nxd4?? Nxd4
lines.intro: In the Short system White's d4 and b2 are both weak after ...Qb6. If White castles carelessly, ...cxd4 and ...Nxd4 win a piece.

moves.text: Attack the base of the chain.
White defends d4 with the bishop.
Attack b2 and add a second attacker on d4.
White develops. But now the d2 knight blocks the queen's view of d4.
Win the pawn: the e3 bishop is now attacked too.
**Blunder (??)**: the d4 knight looks defended by the bishop and the queen, but the queen is blocked by the d2 knight. Better was 9.Bf4.
Take the bishop. The d1 queen cannot recapture because the d2 knight is in the way – you are a full piece up.

lines.summary: Count attackers and defenders on d4 – and check that each defender can really recapture. Here the d2 knight blocked the queen. The ...Qb6/...Nc6/...cxd4 pressure is your main weapon in the Advance.

lines.name: Trap warning: 7.Be3 Nc6 8.dxc5 h5 9.Nf4 hxg4?? 10.Nxg6
lines.intro: In the g4 Advance, taking on g4 looks natural – but it lets White take your bishop and wreck your pawns. Know it so you play 9...Bh7.

moves.text: White defends d4 with the bishop.
White takes and gives up the centre.
**Blunder (??)**: you forget the bishop. Correct was 9...Bh7, keeping the bishop safe.
You must recapture. Your pawns are broken and your king is weak.

lines.summary: Before you take a pawn, check whether your own pieces are attacked. Here the g6 bishop was hanging, so 9...Bh7 was necessary.
